6	- Papers by Spotify researchers (anderson2020algorithmic, mehrotra2018towards, mcinerney2018explore, brost2019music) are **peer-reviewed research**. They describe experiments or datasets. 11	## Ch. 1: „בוקר טוב, נועה" (why recommendation exists; catalog size; choice overload)
12	
13	- Spotify states that its catalog has over 100 million tracks, 8 million podcast titles and 800,000 audiobooks (the last "in select markets"). **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026company | Company-info page: "over 100 million tracks"; "8 million podcast titles"; "800,000 audiobooks in select markets". The figures are undated on the page; accessed 2026-11-14 | Confidence: high (that Spotify says it). Write it as "according to Spotify, as of Nov 2026".
14	- Spotify states that it has 788 million users and 306 million subscribers in 184 markets. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026company | "788 million users"; "306 million subscribers"; "in 184 markets" (undated, accessed 2026-11-14) | Confidence: high (that Spotify says it)
15	- Research literature describes commercial music catalogs as holding tens of millions of pieces. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1 "Particularities of music recommendation", Magnitude of items: "The size of common commercial music catalogs is in the range of tens of millions music pieces" | Confidence: high
16	- Music items are short (about 3–5 minutes), are often consumed in sequence and in the background, and may be enjoyed again when repeated. This sets music recommendation apart from recommending films or books. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | schedl2018current | §2.1: "the duration of music items usually ranges between 3 and 5 minutes"; "Music is often consumed passively, in the background." | Confidence: high
17	- Schwartz argues that a very large number of choices can reduce well-being (the "paradox of choice"). **[GENERAL METHOD: popular-science book]** | schwartz2004paradox | Publishers Weekly review (verified page) describes the thesis: "having all these choices actually goes so far as to erode our psychological well-being." | Confidence: medium. Present this as Schwartz's *argument*, not settled fact (see Gaps).
18	- Spotify publicly states that it personalizes much of what users hear and see. **[PLATFORM CLAIM: Spotify]** | spotify2026understanding | "we personalize much of what you hear and see on Spotify." (page last updated 2026-10-23) | Confidence: high

20	
21	## Ch. 2: „כל דילוג נספר" (explicit vs. implicit feedback; skips)
22	
23	- Implicit feedback means systems passively track behavior (e.g. purchase history, watching habits, browsing). Unlike explicit ratings, it gives no direct statement of what the user likes or dislikes. **[GENERAL METHOD]** | hu2008collaborative | Abstract: "Unlike the much more extensively researched explicit feedback, we do not have any direct input from the users" | Confidence: high
24	- Implicit data should be read as positive *and* negative preference, each held with varying confidence. This is the basis for "a skip ≠ I hate this". **[GENERAL METHOD]** | hu2008collaborative | Abstract: "positive and negative preference associated with vastly varying confidence levels" | Confidence: high
25	- Researchers at Spotify call skip behavior one of "two particularly important forms of implicit feedback" (the other is context switching). **[GENERAL METHOD: peer-reviewed, Spotify-authored dataset paper]** | brost2019music | §4 Dataset Analysis: "two particularly important forms of implicit feedback: user skip behavior, and their context switch behavior" | Confidence: high
26	- The public dataset distinguishes degrees of skipping: played "very briefly", played "briefly", "most of the track was played", or played "in its entirety". 7	
8	A visually designed Hebrew book of about 20 pages that explains how music recommendation systems work. 1	# PRD — „מאחורי הפלייליסט" (Behind the Playlist)
2	
3	*Status: draft v0.2 · 2026-11-11 · Owner: Boss (coordinating agent)*
4	*v0.2: toolchain installed and verified (§10); engine fixed to XeLaTeX; font rule from the Hebrew smoke test (§6); agent definitions created, none run yet (§7).*
5	
6	## 1. Summary
7	
8	A visually designed Hebrew book of about 20 pages that explains how music recommendation systems work. The reader follows a fictional listener through everyday listening situations (morning commute, workout, studying, a party, a breakup playlist...). Each situation introduces one mechanism, explained accessibly with light humor and backed by verifiable research.
9	
10	The book is a university project. Besides the book itself, it must document how it was made: a prompt log and evidence that three specialist agents (Researcher, Writer, Reviewer) worked on it under a coordinating Boss.
11	
12	## 2. Goals and non-goals
13	
14	**Goals**
15	- Explain the main ideas behind music recommendation (collaborative filtering, content and audio features, context and sessions, feedback signals, exploration vs. exploitation, cold start, filter bubbles and diversity) to a non-technical Hebrew reader.
16	- Ground every factual claim in a verifiable, cited source.
17	- Produce a polished, consistent, print-quality PDF with correct right-to-left Hebrew layout.
18	- Make the process reproducible: anyone can rebuild the PDF from source.
19	
20	**Non-goals**
21	- Revealing or reconstructing Spotify's (or any company's) actual production algorithm. Illustrative models are always labelled as educational simplifications.
22	- Training or running a real recommender on real user data.
23	- A general orchestration framework for agents.
24	
25	## 3. Audience and tone
26	
27	- **Audience:** Hebrew-speaking students and curious listeners with no technical or math background beyond high school.
28	- **Tone:** friendly, lightly humorous, never condescending. Humor lives in the listener's story, not in the facts.
29	- **Voice:** the fictional listener's scenes, followed by short explanations, then an emphasis box with the key takeaway.
30

46	## 5. Content requirements
47	
48	### 5.1 Book structure
49	1. **Title page** — Hebrew title „מאחורי הפלייליסט", subtitle, author/course details, a visual element.
50	2. **Abstract (תקציר)** — about half a page.
51	3. **Table of contents.**
52	4. **Chapters** — roughly 5–7 chapters, each built around one listening situation of the fictional listener. Tentative arc (subject to Researcher findings):
53	   - Introduction: meet the listener; why recommendation exists at all.
54	   - Signals: what the system learns from plays, skips, saves, repeats.
55	   - "People like you": collaborative filtering and similarity.
56	   - "Songs like this": content/audio features and metadata.
57	   - Context and sessions: time, activity, sequence.
58	   - Exploration, cold start, and new artists.
59	   - Filter bubbles, diversity, fairness, and what the listener can do.
60	   - Conclusion.
61	5. **Bibliography (מקורות)** — generated by the bibliography tool from `references.bib`.
62	
63	### 5.2 Mandatory elements
64	- **Graph (≥1):** generated by Python/matplotlib from a data file in the repo; Hebrew labels rendered correctly; style matches the book palette. If it uses invented data, the caption says so explicitly.
65	- **Table (≥1):** e.g. the fictional listener's listening log or a comparison of recommendation approaches.
66	- **Formula (≥1):** e.g. cosine similarity between listeners or songs, with:
67	  - a plain-language explanation of every symbol,
68	  - a fully worked numerical example with small numbers,
69	  - a label stating it is an educational formula, not a description of any company's system.
70	- **Eight-block diagram:** the recommendation process (e.g. collect signals → clean/aggregate → represent users & songs → generate candidates → score/rank → filter & diversify → present → collect feedback, looping back). Built in TikZ as editable vector objects, with RTL-correct Hebrew labels.
71	- **Emphasis boxes:** at least three types, used consistently, e.g. „בקצרה" (key takeaway), „רגע, זה אמיתי?" (fact vs. myth / research note), „מעבדה" (formula or worked example), and a distinct style for fictional-data notices.
72	
73	### 5.3 Research and honesty rules
74	- Every factual claim about how recommender systems work, about specific companies, or about research findings cites a source in the bibliography.
75	- Sources must be verifiable: peer-reviewed papers, books, official engineering/research blogs, or reputable journalism. Each `.bib` entry has a DOI or URL where possible.
76	- Aim for at least 10 distinct sources, with at least 4 academic.
77	- Statements about Spotify or other companies are attributed to what that company has publicly said ("according to Spotify's research blog...") and never extrapolated into claims about its actual algorithm.
78	- All fictional listening data, people, and numbers are marked as fictional in the caption or the box where they appear.
79	- No invented citations. The Reviewer checks every cited source against the claim it supports.
80	
81	## 6. Design requirements
82	
83	- **Engine:** XeLaTeX + polyglossia (`bidi`), built with `latexmk -xelatex`; bibliography with biblatex + biber. Verified by the smoke test `tests/hebrew-sample/` (§10).
84	- **Font rule (from the smoke test):** Arial Hebrew has no Latin glyphs, and math and Latin text use `\setmainfont`. The main font must therefore cover Latin, and Hebrew runs use `\hebrewfont`. Every build must have **0 "Missing character" lines** in the log.
85	- **TikZ RTL rule:** TikZ typesets node text in a left-to-right `\hbox`, where `\setRTL` has no effect, so multi-word Hebrew labels come out in reversed word order. All Hebrew TikZ nodes use the `heb` style from `style.sty` (`execute at begin node=\beginR, execute at end node=\endR`). Inside a `heb` node, any colour change (`text=<color>` or `\color`) renders the text **white**, so coloured Hebrew node text uses `\hebcolor{<color>}{<text>}` without `heb`, which keeps the colour outside the RTL segment, and the source text stays in natural order. **Verification rule:** word order in the PDF is checked numerically, from **glyph** x-positions (PyMuPDF `rawdict`; its word-level extraction reorders RTL strings itself), so that in RTL the first word lies to the right of the next, and not by reading a rendered image alone.
86	- **Direction:** all running text, headings, TOC, captions, lists, and bibliography read right-to-left; embedded English terms and numbers render correctly in LTR.
87	- **Typography:** one Hebrew body font, one Hebrew heading font (or weights of the same family), one Latin companion font; fonts are licensed for this use and named in the README.
88	- **Color palette:** 3–4 named colors defined once in the style file and used for headings, boxes, the diagram, and the graph.
89	- **Layout:** A4 or B5, comfortable margins, line spacing about 1.2–1.4, no overfull lines visible in the PDF, no widows of headings at page bottoms, figures close to their reference.
90	- **Consistency:** all boxes, captions, and chapter openers share one style defined in a single style file.
91	
92	## 7. Process and agent roles
93	
94	| Role | Responsibility | Main outputs |
95	|---|---|---|
96	| **Boss** (main session) | Plans, writes briefs, integrates, builds the PDF, keeps logs, talks to the user | PRD, logs, LaTeX integration, build |
97	| **Researcher** | Finds and verifies sources; writes a fact sheet with claim → source pairs | `docs/agents/research-notes.md`, `book/references.bib` |
98	| **Writer** | Writes Hebrew chapter text from the outline and fact sheet only | chapter `.tex` files |
99	| **Reviewer** | Checks facts against sources, labelling of fictional data, Hebrew quality, and the rendered PDF against this PRD | `docs/agents/review-*.md` with issues and verdict |
100	
101	Agents are defined in `.claude/agents/{researcher,writer,reviewer}.md` and run through Claude Code's built-in Agent tool, using the existing Claude login with no orchestration framework. They hand work to each other through files in `docs/agents/`, not through long prompts. The planned budget is about 5–6 calls in total. A definition file existing does not count as a run.
102	
103	Every agent call is recorded in `docs/agents/log.md` (date, agent, brief, files read, files produced, outcome). User prompts are recorded verbatim in `docs/prompts.md`; no earlier exchanges are invented.
104	
105	## 8. Acceptance criteria
106	
107	The project is done when all of the following hold:
108	
109	1. `build/behind-the-playlist.pdf` builds from a clean checkout with one documented command and no LaTeX errors.
110	2. The PDF has 18–24 pages, including a title page, abstract, TOC, chapters, and bibliography in this order.
111	3. Hebrew text, headings, TOC, captions, and bibliography are right-to-left; mixed English/numbers render in the correct order (checked visually on every page).
